The Princess of Wales is set to embark on her first official overseas engagement since completing cancer treatment, with a visit to northern Italy next week. Kate will travel to Reggio Emilia to observe how local communities, in the aftermath of the Second World War, ingeniously repurposed abandoned military equipment, including a tank, to establish a globally influential model of early-years education.

The visit will highlight the origins of the renowned "Reggio Emilia approach." Following the war, residents – many of them women – financed some of Italy’s inaugural nursery schools by selling scrap metal salvaged from equipment left behind by retreating German forces. These pioneering efforts laid the groundwork for the educational philosophy, which is now influential worldwide and aligns closely with Kate’s focus on children’s social and emotional wellbeing.

The wife of the heir to the throne, Prince William, and mother of three, launched the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood in 2021. This initiative aims to consolidate expertise and research within the field of early childhood development. The trip, scheduled for 13 to 14 May, marks a significant return to international duties for the Princess.

"Some time ago, British representatives visited our city and our early childhood education services, and shortly afterwards we heard of the Princess’s interest in coming ‌to see us," Marwa Mahmoud, Reggio Emilia’s councillor for education, told ‌Reuters. Italian officials said Kate's interest was focused on the historical roots of Reggio’s schools, their public character, the role of women, the link between nature and education, and strong community involvement.

open image in gallery The Princess of Wales meets families with babies and young children to discuss research during the launch of 'Foundations for Life: A Guide to Social and Emotional Development' ( Reuters )

The medium-sized city of Reggio Emilia has one ⁠of the highest levels of preschool participation in Italy, with enrolment among children aged three to six close to universal and attendance at infant-toddler services more than twice the national average.

Here, pioneering schools for children under six took shape decades before a national law followed in 1968. In the Reggio Emilia approach the child is seen as an active learner, with the potential to explore and understand the world through many forms of expression – often described by educators as the “hundred languages” of children.

Classes are organised ‌around communal spaces known as piazzas, with in-house kitchens and ateliers where children are encouraged ​to experiment with materials, colours, and sounds.

Today, Reggio Emilia has 89 infant-toddler centres ‌and preschools, most operated by the municipality or ⁠the state, with fees set according to family income.

International attention grew after U.S. magazine ⁠Newsweek cited a Reggio Emilia preschool among the world’s top ten schools in 1991.

"For years, Britain looked to Reggio Emilia as a ‌model, with hundreds of teachers ​visiting annually," said Maddalena Tedeschi, president of Reggio Children, ‌an international centre that promotes research. "Policy changes and ​funding cuts in the UK later reduced travel, but interest remained and evolved into new forms of exchange."

News.title: Local election results live: Farage’s Reform delivers huge blow to Labour but Starmer vows not to quit
News.content:
Starmer vows he won't resign as Labour hit by 'really tough' local election results

Sir Keir Starmer says he is “hurt” but is “not going to walk away” after Labour lost hundreds of councillor seats, along with control of eight councils, in the local elections.

With more than 40 of the 136 council results in, the party appears to be losing grip of its historic heartlands with major losses in Tameside, Hartlepool and Wigan, as pollsters predict more than 1,500 Labour council seats could be lost.

Meanwhile, Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party has seen a surge in support, winning more than 300 seats, and the Green Party has won the Hackney mayoral election, ousting Labour.

Speaking on Friday morning, Sir Keir said: “The voters have sent a message about the pace of change, how they want their lives improved. I was elected to meet those challenges but I’m not going to walk away from those challenges.”

According to The Times, before polls closed Mr Miliband had privately urged the prime minister to set out a timetable for his departure after the elections, while Hartlepool MP Jonathan Brash, whose wife Pamela Hargreaves lost her seat in Reform’s clean sweep, said Sir Keir should go.

News.title: Gadget Show host Jason Bradbury on AI: ‘It is an incredible moment in our history’
News.content:
We’ve covered an extensive amount of technology here at Telegraph Recommended, from the latest smartphones and laptops to voice-activated kitchen bins. There are a lot of products on the market, but one person who knows how to sort the wheat from the chaff is Jason Bradbury.

The tech expert is best known for presenting Channel 5’s technology programme The Gadget Show for 12 years. He’s also the author of a series of techno-thrillers for children, and has also been on the judging panels for the BAFTA Video Games Awards and the MediaGuardian Innovation Awards.

We sat down with Bradbury at the Ideal Home Show in Birmingham, where he curated the smart home showcase, for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer queries from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel. Read his answers below.

Is there a best time of year to purchase new gadgets?

Boris, North West

Yes. Often, new technology is showcased in January and is sometimes revisited in summer, then is available to buy in the autumn. That means September, October or November is the best time to buy new tech, like games consoles, virtual reality helmets or new smartphones.

If you were on a desert island, which gadget would you miss the most?

My Onewheel. As the name suggests, it’s a single wheel with a skateboard built around it. It’s the closest you’ll get to being like Marty McFly in Back To The Future. At the ripe age of 57 years old, this is my daily driver. When I’ve taken my kids to school, I jump on my skateboard and glide down into town. I live in Newquay, Cornwall, and while you can go on the beach with it, it’s got to be a flat beach. A desert island isn’t going to be ideal.

Do you prefer iPhone or Android devices?

This is a political question for which 50 per cent of the population are going to hate me. In fact, a larger proportion of people actually have Android devices.

I love both for different reasons, and both have amazing features to offer. The walled garden that is the iPhone is a coherent operating system, but you can’t put stuff on or get stuff off it easily, which Android is great for.

Are we pushing technology into areas of the home that don’t need it?

Anthony, Yorkshire

There’s nothing wrong with an AI feature-rich bird table. We may be pushing technology into areas of the home that it never belonged in, but it’s a choice. We get pressured to buy the shiniest new thing, but it’s easy to go off grid. I have a campervan, and while yes I plug it in to charge the battery, it’s pretty much off grid. I could take an Xbox with me, but I don’t.

If you choose to buy technology that enhances life for you, that’s great. Take the bird feeder example – this one at the Ideal Home Show uses AI to identify the species of bird that’s nibbling on the seeds that you put out. If you’re not as mobile as you used to be, you get to interact with your garden in a way that you wouldn’t ordinarily be able to. Someone else would say that was a ridiculous idea.

It’s an exciting time. I like where smart tech is going. In the health area, it could be seen as an intrusion, collecting the most intimate data around your body. But it’s important to know where your health is so you can take action and own it.

What are your tech predictions for the next few years?

Brian, London

AI is going to bring us new materials. There will be efficiency gains in the recovery of thermal energy, with benefits for fuel efficiency. We’ll see new types of polymers and non-polluting plastics, with gains through AI in biology to make organisms that can consume plastic. This will hopefully solve microplastic pollution – a dreadful problem in Cornwall. There will also be advances in surgery, identifying disease in treatment and pharmacology.

I understand people’s jobs are at risk from AI, and that’s a real consequence. But if you stop the cynicism for a minute, it is an incredible moment in our history. I feel privileged to be gazing through the window of the next two years and beyond. We could be looking at fusion reactors efficient enough to work properly, self-driving vehicles that will make travel safer and more efficient, new fuels… It’s mind-blowing.

When did your interest in tech begin?

Daniel, London

My father, who was a plastics expert working for a factory, brought home a prototype for the first generation of digital watches and calculators.

I was born in 1969, and it was an amazing time to be alive. Growing up and being conscious of tech in the 70s and 80s felt similar to how it does now. The ‘70s was quite analogue before the mass adoption of consumer electronics, computers and video games. The fervour around new ideas, born of the obsession and efficiency gains with AI, is a similar feeling to the 80s.

Who was your biggest inspiration?

Ekaterina, West Midlands

My father. He was a huge fan of technology and insisted on buying me computers and first-generation consoles. He got me to try programming and be connected to the world in which he was making prototypes for the new computer generation.

There’s also Sir Clive Sinclair, who was the ‘80s answer to Elon Musk, if Elon Musk was ginger and looked like a geography teacher. He was the brains behind the first computer that a lot of British kids in the 80s got their hands on, the ZX80, ZX81 and the ZX Spectrum. I actually own the Sinclair C5 vehicle from 1985, although I don’t drive it too often because it’s not that reliable.

Does having a smart home pose any security risks?

Liam, London

Yes. When you install cameras and smart devices that track you, there is, without a shadow of a doubt, a consideration there around who does what with that data. When everything’s connected, someone can hack it. There are efforts every minute of every day to grab your personal information to monetise it. You need to consider that, especially with AI, which is great at writing code, hacking and putting that power in the hands of all kinds of people.

What I’d say on that score is to get a router with good security, and don’t go with default passwords.

What’s your ‘take’ on children and gadgets?

Patricia, West Midlands

As the father of three crazy young people, one of whom is a professional Fortnite player, I have an open attitude to technology. But I also don’t like seeing kids in restaurants staring at an iPad. I also understand the pressures that parents have and I’m guilty of doing the same thing. Sometimes you’ve been up all night with a baby, so your toddler gets the iPad instead of you.

I don’t think people need me to patronise them and tell them what they already know, which is that technology is empowering, wonderful and fun, but when it’s sunny outside, get out there and get dirty. It’s all about balance.

News.title: They seek riches from the jungle – but this eco-system is our future
News.content:
As the sun sinks over the Sangha river in a far corner of the Congo Basin, the village chief contemplates the future of his homeland. “The resources will finish, but after that, then what?” asks Gabriel Mobolambi. His village, Bomassa, is the gateway to Nouabalé-Ndoki National Park – a vast stretch of largely unspoilt jungle.

Like many who live in this remote region, he has had to weigh up the benefits of resource exploitation against conservation. The region is rich in precious metals and gems which promise riches – but Mobolambi, a responsible leader, takes a longer view.

“There are gold and diamonds in the forest, but conservation is dependable,” he says. Behind him, fishermen cast their nets into the fast-flowing water. Mobolambi is part of a network of indigenous communities who believe that conserving their pristine environment is a safer bet for long-term prosperity. Their work has ramifications that could extend well beyond this vast wilderness.

Gabriel Mobolambi, the chief of Bomassa village, on the boundary of Nouabalé-Ndoki Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Elephants bathe at the Mbeli bai forest clearing, the site of a long term scientific survey Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

The tributaries of the Congo River system reach into nine countries; its twists and turns nourish forests and swamps that trap more carbon than even the Amazon region. It is in the Republic of Congo that these jungles are at their most impressive, covering well over half of the country and sheltering endangered species.

The region has known decades of insecurity. Mobolambi still remembers the 1997 civil war, when armed militias from across central Africa would arrive to hunt elephants amid the chaos, exchanging gifts with local chiefs for the right to leave with plundered ivory. “It was a strange conflict,” he says, “but now we wear the same scent.”

Research groups monitor the bais, which reveal wildlife that is usually hidden in the dense forest Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham/The Telegraph

Despite this new calm, in the past two decades, the Republic of Congo has lost over a million hectares of tree cover.

Walking with a research team, we leave the village of Bomassa on foot. The terrain is difficult, and a few miles into the permanent shadows of the tall tree canopy it swiftly turns into a muddy endurance sport. Researchers, including Aristide Mouele of Wildlife Conservation Society, from the coastal city of Pointe-Noire, often have to use canoes to access campsites deep in the jungle.

“These ecosystems create the second lung of the world,” explains Mouele, who has been working at Nouabalé-Ndoki since 2017, running a study project at one of the park’s natural forest clearings, known locally as bais.

Our movement from a campsite to an observation platform at the bai must be made in watchful groups, and only in daylight hours, with all eyes kept peeled for any elephants that could be startled and charge.

Arriving in the open bai reveals a world of life that would be invisible in the undergrowth.

Western lowland gorillas cautiously peer out from the treeline, then roll into the thick fronds of grass, while groups of forest elephants greet each other with excitable flapping of trunks and tails.

A river flows through the bai, and a crocodile can suddenly be seen gliding through the clearing.

This bai has been monitored since way back in 1995, and every individual animal visiting the area has been logged. “The animals maintain the ecosystem,” says Mouele. “The bai is a summary of the health of the forest.”

A forest elephant moves through the jungle of Nouabale-Ndoki Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham An infant western lowland gorilla in the jungle close to the Mondika research camp Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

Elephants that graze here spread seeds throughout the Congo Basin, as they pass across international borders.

Though emblematic species such as gorillas, chimpanzees and forest elephants attract the most interest and funding, researchers on the ground still find time for less glamorous yet critical climate science. Mouele’s project, a study of animal behaviour, is a labour of love, and he has spent countless nights sleeping on a spartan observation deck, eating tinned rations and sheltering from rainstorms.

Other long-term studies are underway here to assess the health of the forest. At the twin research sites of Mondika and Goualougo, both in the Nouabalé-Ndoki park, around 1,000 individual trees are visited and inspected each month, a painstaking process that requires up to six days of hiking in the forest and minute observations, tallying leaves and fallen fruits, recording growth, scars and signs of disease.

Researcher Gaston Abea walks through a swarm of butterflies at the Mondika research campsite Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Tracker Nelson Mobolambi, the village chief ’s son, manoeuvres his canoe Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

The study’s remit is to reveal long-term trends, and its data will highlight the effects of changing temperatures on fruiting, flowering and seed dispersal.

While Mouele was trained at the Marien Ngouabi University in Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, the majority of the trackers who work at the park are from Ba’aka indigenous hunter-gatherer communities, the original inhabitants of the region.

A forest elephant moves through the jungle – researchers must be careful not to startle them Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham/The Telegraph

Gaston Abea is a Ba’aka, and the first member of an indigenous community to become a published academic author, for his observations of gorilla behaviour in the forests of Nouabalé-Ndoki. “The forest is our school of life,” he says. “I have six children and will bring them all here to learn the traditions of our ancestors.”

The jungle seems less impenetrable when he walks through it, pointing out herbs and shoots that have medical uses. “We can spend 21 days in the forest, we carry 20kg packs and stop every 500 metres to map all the species of tree and animal we see or any damage,” explains Abea.

These indigenous communities have long been marginalised and targeted during conflicts across the Congo Basin. Over 60,000 Mbuti pygmies were killed in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) during the Second Congo War in the early 2000s.

Working in conservation has helped keep the culture of these groups alive; their traditional survival skills and ability to navigate the forests are of vital importance for modern research.

The low population density of the Republic of Congo has saved it from many of the issues faced in DRC, where millions more are dependent on the shrinking resources of the land.

Trackers hike through the forests of Nouabale-Ndoki Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham A barge carrying hundreds of logs travels downstream on the Congo river. Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

Industrial exploitation is increasing though, and the road that leads from Nouabalé-Ndoki to the trading town of Ouesso is lined with flatbed trucks piled with bulbous logs. Conditions have dramatically changed since then, and when they are felled, they will be the last of their kind.

News.title: Oil jumps back above $100 as US and Iran trade missile fire
News.content:
Oil prices rose back above $100 a barrel as the US and Iran exchanged missile fire in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose as much as 2.9pc to nearly $103 as the fragile ceasefire faced its most serious test.

Crude had dropped down as low as $96 on Thursday but lurched upwards after US forces carried out strikes on Iranian military targets in response to an attack on three American destroyers in the Strait.

Stocks fell sharply overnight, with the main indexes in Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong all down more than 1pc.

President Donald Trump said the strikes on Iran were “just a love tap” and insisted the ceasefire was still in effect.

Iran is yet to announce its response to a US proposal setting out the terms for ending the conflict.

Read the latest updates below.

News.title: Prince William celebrates wildly as Unai Emery shows he is still Europa League king
News.content:
Nottingham Forest take a one-goal advantage into the second leg of the all-English Europa League semi-final with Aston Villa at Villa Park. Chris Wood’s penalty following Lucas Digne’s handball gives Forest the lead coming into tonight’s second leg.

In between the two legs of this semi-final, Aston Villa lost 2-1 at home to Tottenham on Sunday to remain fifth in the Premier League. Unai Emery has won the Europa League as a manager on four occasions, the most of any manager, but is still looking to win his first trophy in charge at Aston Villa as he approaches four years in charge at the club.

“Each momentum is different, and as well in different competitions,” Emery said. “But every different experience we have should help us for days like tomorrow [tonight]. But today is our first one [semi-final] here playing one match. We played Conference League semi-final two years ago, but first leg at home, second leg away. Last year in the Champions League quarter-final it was the second leg at home but it was a quarter-final. Tomorrow [tonight], this match is special. It is different. We are playing in Villa Park. They have the advantage. For this reason for me they are the favourites. Tomorrow [tonight] we have a huge opportunity to enjoy momentum, to enjoy competing.”

Emery has confirmed that midfielder Amadou Onana will miss tonight’s game but John McGinn is set to be available.

Nottingham Forest took another big step to Premier League safety in between these two legs as they beat Chelsea 3-1 at Stamford Bridge on Bank Holiday Monday to move six points clear of the relegation zone with three games remaining. Vitor Pereira’s side come into this fixture in good form as they are currently on a 10-match unbeaten run in all competitions.

“Tomorrow [tonight] is a day to enjoy and to compete,” Pereira said. “We need to prove ourselves again. This is something to be grateful for, because we will be in a semi-final to try and reach a final, and we are there. It is a moment to show our mentality, that we are resilient and that we can compete from the first minute until the last minute in a fantastic atmosphere. I just want to be proud of my players, supporters and myself.

“The most difficult moments of my personal life were the moments that I became stronger. When we suffer, we remember the pain. When we remember the pain, we do everything to not feel that again. This is fire within us and, sometimes in life, this is powerful, when we want to prove ourselves. This is a moment for my players, because they have had tough moments this season, to not feel the pressure to win this competition, but to try and be the best version of themselves.”

Morgan Gibbs-White is a major doubt having been involved in a heavy collision with Chelsea goalkeeper Robert Sanchez on Monday, which required plenty of stitches. Gibbs-White is one of a number of doubts for Forest coming into this game, including Ibrahim Sangare, Ola Aina, Murillo and Dan Ndoye.

The winner of this tie will face either Freiburg or Braga in the final. Team news to follow shortly.

News.title: They seek riches from the jungle – but this eco-system is our future
News.content:
As the sun sinks over the Sangha river in a far corner of the Congo Basin, the village chief contemplates the future of his homeland. “The resources will finish, but after that, then what?” asks Gabriel Mobolambi. His village, Bomassa, is the gateway to Nouabalé-Ndoki National Park – a vast stretch of largely unspoilt jungle.

Like many who live in this remote region, he has had to weigh up the benefits of resource exploitation against conservation. The region is rich in precious metals and gems which promise riches – but Mobolambi, a responsible leader, takes a longer view.

“There are gold and diamonds in the forest, but conservation is dependable,” he says. Behind him, fishermen cast their nets into the fast-flowing water. Mobolambi is part of a network of indigenous communities who believe that conserving their pristine environment is a safer bet for long-term prosperity. Their work has ramifications that could extend well beyond this vast wilderness.

Gabriel Mobolambi, the chief of Bomassa village, on the boundary of Nouabalé-Ndoki Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Elephants bathe at the Mbeli bai forest clearing, the site of a long term scientific survey Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

The tributaries of the Congo River system reach into nine countries; its twists and turns nourish forests and swamps that trap more carbon than even the Amazon region. It is in the Republic of Congo that these jungles are at their most impressive, covering well over half of the country and sheltering endangered species.

The region has known decades of insecurity. Mobolambi still remembers the 1997 civil war, when armed militias from across central Africa would arrive to hunt elephants amid the chaos, exchanging gifts with local chiefs for the right to leave with plundered ivory. “It was a strange conflict,” he says, “but now we wear the same scent.”

Research groups monitor the bais, which reveal wildlife that is usually hidden in the dense forest Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham/The Telegraph

Despite this new calm, in the past two decades, the Republic of Congo has lost over a million hectares of tree cover.

Walking with a research team, we leave the village of Bomassa on foot. The terrain is difficult, and a few miles into the permanent shadows of the tall tree canopy it swiftly turns into a muddy endurance sport. Researchers, including Aristide Mouele of Wildlife Conservation Society, from the coastal city of Pointe-Noire, often have to use canoes to access campsites deep in the jungle.

“These ecosystems create the second lung of the world,” explains Mouele, who has been working at Nouabalé-Ndoki since 2017, running a study project at one of the park’s natural forest clearings, known locally as bais.

Our movement from a campsite to an observation platform at the bai must be made in watchful groups, and only in daylight hours, with all eyes kept peeled for any elephants that could be startled and charge.

Arriving in the open bai reveals a world of life that would be invisible in the undergrowth.

Western lowland gorillas cautiously peer out from the treeline, then roll into the thick fronds of grass, while groups of forest elephants greet each other with excitable flapping of trunks and tails.

A river flows through the bai, and a crocodile can suddenly be seen gliding through the clearing.

This bai has been monitored since way back in 1995, and every individual animal visiting the area has been logged. “The animals maintain the ecosystem,” says Mouele. “The bai is a summary of the health of the forest.”

A forest elephant moves through the jungle of Nouabale-Ndoki Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham An infant western lowland gorilla in the jungle close to the Mondika research camp Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

Elephants that graze here spread seeds throughout the Congo Basin, as they pass across international borders.

Though emblematic species such as gorillas, chimpanzees and forest elephants attract the most interest and funding, researchers on the ground still find time for less glamorous yet critical climate science. Mouele’s project, a study of animal behaviour, is a labour of love, and he has spent countless nights sleeping on a spartan observation deck, eating tinned rations and sheltering from rainstorms.

Other long-term studies are underway here to assess the health of the forest. At the twin research sites of Mondika and Goualougo, both in the Nouabalé-Ndoki park, around 1,000 individual trees are visited and inspected each month, a painstaking process that requires up to six days of hiking in the forest and minute observations, tallying leaves and fallen fruits, recording growth, scars and signs of disease.

Researcher Gaston Abea walks through a swarm of butterflies at the Mondika research campsite Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham Tracker Nelson Mobolambi, the village chief ’s son, manoeuvres his canoe Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

The study’s remit is to reveal long-term trends, and its data will highlight the effects of changing temperatures on fruiting, flowering and seed dispersal.

While Mouele was trained at the Marien Ngouabi University in Brazzaville, the capital of the Republic of Congo, the majority of the trackers who work at the park are from Ba’aka indigenous hunter-gatherer communities, the original inhabitants of the region.

A forest elephant moves through the jungle – researchers must be careful not to startle them Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham/The Telegraph

Gaston Abea is a Ba’aka, and the first member of an indigenous community to become a published academic author, for his observations of gorilla behaviour in the forests of Nouabalé-Ndoki. “The forest is our school of life,” he says. “I have six children and will bring them all here to learn the traditions of our ancestors.”

The jungle seems less impenetrable when he walks through it, pointing out herbs and shoots that have medical uses. “We can spend 21 days in the forest, we carry 20kg packs and stop every 500 metres to map all the species of tree and animal we see or any damage,” explains Abea.

These indigenous communities have long been marginalised and targeted during conflicts across the Congo Basin. Over 60,000 Mbuti pygmies were killed in the neighbouring Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) during the Second Congo War in the early 2000s.

Working in conservation has helped keep the culture of these groups alive; their traditional survival skills and ability to navigate the forests are of vital importance for modern research.

The low population density of the Republic of Congo has saved it from many of the issues faced in DRC, where millions more are dependent on the shrinking resources of the land.

Trackers hike through the forests of Nouabale-Ndoki Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham A barge carrying hundreds of logs travels downstream on the Congo river. Credit : Hugh Kinsella Cunningham

Industrial exploitation is increasing though, and the road that leads from Nouabalé-Ndoki to the trading town of Ouesso is lined with flatbed trucks piled with bulbous logs. Along the Congo River, barges can frequently be seen travelling with hundreds of cut trees destined for sawmills downstream or for sale into opaque supply chains.

Many of the largest old-growth trees here date back 900 years. “These trees are rare, and do not replace easily. They grew when the forest was more open and lighter,” says Dr David Morgan, of Lincoln Park Zoo in Chicago, another of Nouabalé-Ndoki’s visiting researchers.

Conditions have dramatically changed since then, and when they are felled, they will be the last of their kind.

News.title: Trump: Iran strikes are just a love tap
News.content:
Donald Trump said strikes on Iran were “just a love tap” after the US and Tehran traded attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.

The US military confirmed it struck targets in the strait after Iran launched “unprovoked” missile, drone and small boat attacks on three American destroyers transiting the waterway.

In a phone call with ABC News on Thursday evening, the US president said of the assault against Iranian military targets: “It’s just a love tap.”

In a post on Truth Social, Mr Trump added that several Iranian small boats had been “completely destroyed” after firing on the destroyers, which sustained no damage and successfully transited out of the strait.

The US president said the US vessels – identified as the USS Truxtun, USS Rafael Peralta and USS Mason – would rejoin the American naval blockade in the strait.

When asked if the attack meant an end to the fragile ceasefire, which has been in place since April 7, Mr Trump said: “No, no, the ceasefire is going. It’s in effect.”

However, the US president warned that if Tehran did not quickly agree to a deal, the US military would “knock them out a lot harder, and a lot more violently, in the future”.

Iran’s top joint military command had earlier accused the US of violating the ceasefire and threatened to “respond powerfully”, as the truce teetered on the edge of collapse.

US Central Command (Centcom) said it targeted Iranian military facilities, including missile and drone launch sites, which it claimed were utilised in assaults on US forces.

Strikes were carried out on the city of Bandar Abbas, located north of the critical sea passage, and the Qeshm Island port.

Sports.title: Man Utd files: £70m star to let wife decide transfer destination as Youth Cup final descends into further chaos
Sports.content:
MANCHESTER UNTIED players danced all night at a concert this week.

Benjamin Sesko was backed up by United defenders Diogo Dalot and Lisandro Martinez at an Akon concert in Manchester.



The trio were spotted singing along, dancing and filming the performance under the stage lights.



Sesko and Dalot were particularly animated, while Martínez was also visible enjoying the atmosphere on Wednesday night.

All three reported to first team training on Thursday morning to prepare for the trip to Sunderland.

PACK A CASE

CASEMIRO is handing the reins to his wife when it comes to picking his next destination.

Well-placed sources say the Brazilian, 34, wants repay his wife for her unwavering support throughout his stints in Madrid and Manchester.

Casemiro is 100 per cent leaving Old Trafford after the next three games against the Black Cats, Nottingham Forest and Brighton.

Under the terms of the contract, Casemiro would automatically trigger a 12-month extension if he reaches 35 starts for the season in the final three matches, but he has agreed to waive that clause.

It was noted that he and his wife Anna have been travelling to Florida during breaks over the years.



DEVIL WEARS…

SEVERAL United players were involved in a photoshoot at Salford Lads’ Club on Wednesday.

Senne Lammens, Matheus Cunha, Amad, Leny Yoro and Martinez posed for United’s new 2026/2027 kit launch video.

Mancunian duo Aitch and Angry Ginge linked up with the squad and will both star in the new release, filmed at the Grade II-listed youth club.

United’s new home kit will go on sale on May 14 and Michael Carrick’s side will debut it in their next home game against Nottingham Forest.

The home kit features a polo collar, while the away jersey returns to a royal blue colour scheme, reminiscent of kits from the late 1980s. Meanwhile, the third kit is inspired by the Lancashire Rose.



FIXTURE FALLOUT

AFTER the fallout from the FA Youth Cup, more chaos is on the horizon for United’s Under 21s.

The winner of Friday’s U21 semi-final against City will travel to either Spurs or Brighton for the final, which is scheduled for next weekend.

The dates given by the Premier League for the final initially are between Friday May 15 and Monday May 18.

However, that will surely have to move now that the Youth Cup final is the day before, unless one club is forced to play a weakened team for one of their finals.



United youngsters Chido Obi and Jim Thwaites and City’s Reigan Heskey and Ryan McAidoo are among the players who would be wanted by both their Under-18s and Under-21s managers.

Last year’s final between City and Southampton ended up being played later than the original dates and only confirmed a day before it took place after a disagreement over where it should be held.

SPECIAL BRU

ANOTHER week and another high-profile interview for Bruno Fernandes, who held court with Gary Neville.

The chat was headlined on the United captain “opening up on turning down summer transfer in favour of Old Trafford stay”. Fernandes first spoke extensively on that matter to dedicated journalists in late October.

Fernandes is a great interviewee and, through no fault of his own, is sounding repetitive as interviewers go over ground that has already been covered. Fernandes gave chapter-and-verse on the Saudi interest to six of us at Carrington on the eve of his 300th United appearance.



Neville was at Carrington for a high-profile interview two years ago when he had a one-on-one with Erik ten Hag.

Ten Hag and his allies dedicated that Thursday afternoon to a PR charm offensive amid the club hierarchy’s barely concealed plans to sack him. The Dutchman generously held court with a handful of journalists off the record.

With Fernandes, it is more campaigning in awards season, not dissimilar to an actor or director jet-setting in an effort to boost their chances of an Academy Award.

Wayne Rooney, United’s last recipient of the Professional Footballers’ Association and Football Writers’ Association gongs in 2010, spoke to Fernandes at Carrington two weeks ago.



It was Rooney’s first interview and eyewitnesses say he was genuinely nervous beforehand but had prepared diligently.

JOY FOR JJ

JJ Gabriel’s inclusion in first-team training on Wednesday was perhaps his most significant yet.

United under 21s have been preparing for Friday night’s derby at City but Gabriel was the only non-senior squad member drafted in.

Carrick has a near fully-fit squad to choose from against Sunderland, with only Matthijs de Ligt definitely out. Benjamin Sesko is also a doubt.

It speaks volumes of how much United value the 15-year-old Gabriel that he was summoned for the midweek session in the absence of Sesko.



THANK HEAVENS FOR EVANS

UNITED were so short of numbers that Jonny Evans, who retired last year, was involved in their midweek session.

With Matthijs de Ligt still recovering from a back problem that has sidelined him for more than five months and the under 21s focused on the derby, the 38-year-old Evans pulled on a bib to get involved in the drills.

FASTER THAN HOT CAKES

THE paltry allocation of 968 tickets United fans received for next week’s FA Youth Cup final at the Joie Stadium sold out in a minute.

Tickets went on sale at 10am on Thursday morning and went faster than the proverbial hot cakes.

The Joie Stadium holds 7,000 (including its standing area). United attracted a crowd of 67,492 for the 2022 final at Old Trafford.



NO WAVE FOR DAVE

SIR Dave Brailsford’s exit as a United director was not even worthy of mention on the club’s investors portal.

Brailsford’s termination as a director was confirmed through United’s filings on Companies House on Thursday, with his departure date listed as April 30.

The United programme for the visit of Liverpool on Sunday still listed Brailsford as a director, though they will have gone to press before news emerged that he had severed all ties with United.

Shortly after his minority stake in United was confirmed in February 2024, Sir Jim Ratcliffe said: “I’ve known Dave now for quite a few years and it’s for good reasons.

“He is obsessive about performance in elite sports, and he is going to be very successful at Manchester United.”



In 2023, Brailsford told former England Test captain Nasser Hussain he was “no expert in football”. It showed.

SOUS YOU

IF you’re a culinary connoisseur, United could have the job just for you.

United are on the lookout for a new sous chef to work at the club’s Carrington training complex.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The successful candidate will manage day-to-day kitchen operations and provide innovative menus “in a motivated team committed to performance nutrition, service, and quality”.



Head chef Will Carvalho and nutritionist Filipe Sousa are a handful of Portuguese backroom staff members still at United after the departure of Ruben Amorim and his coaches.

Sports.title: ‘He can’t be serious’ – Chelsea star, 23, held back by team-mate as he confronts furious fans after being roundly booed
Sports.content:
SOON-TO-BE Chelsea star Emmanuel Emegha felt the full force of the Strasbourg ultras – despite trying to calm them down.

Club captain Emegha, 23, missed Thursday’s Conference League semi-final second leg at home to Rayo Vallecano as Strasbourg were dumped out.





Gary O’Neil‘s side lost 1-0 in both matches, leaving the passionate French fans furious.

As the players went over to applaud them at full-time, they were greeted by jeers and cries of anger.

It led to an awkward confrontation for the baby-faced squad – Europe‘s youngest for the second season in a row – as they clapped the fans but got very little love back.

In an attempt to cool the tensions, Emegha – dressed in black trousers, a big black coat, sunglasses despite the game being played at night, and a giant necklace – moved away from the Strasbourg players, towards the fans.



Former Blues left-back Ben Chilwell and flop Diego Moreira both started to gesture for the supporters to calm down with hand signals.

Moreira, in particular, was bemused by the reception the players were getting.

But Emegha went a step further, striding out with his arm stretched in front, calling for a different response.

He was met with whistles and more disillusioned shouts as Moreira tried to pull him back.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Dutch striker Emegha had a word with his team-mate before taking off the shades and going back to the fans.

He pointed to the stands and then to himself, opening out his arms towards the players.

Contrary to some reports online, it looked like he was pleading for the ultras to pay their respects to the players – not throwing them under the bus.

Emegha appeared to want the fans to clap their efforts rather than digging them out.



He did not get very far as things continued to get worse.

Emegha and the players did then show their appreciation for the fans, clapping strongly, although Moreira stormed off.

Young goalie Mike Penders, another who will return to Chelsea this summer, also had a chat with Emegha before clapping.

And Emegha was quick to come out and address the ugly scenes afterwards.

He wrote on Instagram: “Painful night. Not the ending we wanted, because we dreamed of reaching the Final.



“My only thought at the end was for my teammates to be respected for the effort they have for Strasbourg.

“People can be unhappy with me – I understand the disappointment and frustration, no problem.

“But this team does not deserve that treatment after giving everything for the badge and reaching the semifinals for the first time.

“I am proud of this team and of the journey made together in Europe.

“In the end, we win together, we lose together, and we keep respect for each other.



The Chelsea Blueprint on YouTube Calling all Chelsea fans - we have a brand new YouTube channel! The Sun’s Chelsea YouTube channel will be your go-to destination for the latest news, transfer updates, match previews, post-match analysis, exclusive interviews, fan reactions, and breaking stories from Stamford Bridge. Subscribe to The Chelsea Blueprint on YouTube now

“Thank you to everyone who supported us throughout this run.”

But Chelsea fans, who are preparing to welcome Emegha to Stamford Bridge over the summer, were not impressed by his actions.

One wrote online: “What is this thing with players having to stand there for minutes after a loss? Just clap and get down the tunnel”.

Another added: “He’s gonna fit in perfectly with our no accountability culture”.



A third said: “This guy is the captain apparently and is coming to us in the summer. Another stinky attitude to add to the changing room.”

Someone else commented: “He can’t be f****** serious. He’s playing for my club next season tears.”

Emegha joined Strasbourg in 2023 from Sturm Graz – a prolific producer of excellent No9s in recent years – but was confirmed as moving to Chelsea at the end of this season midway through the campaign.

That raised a storm with Strasbourg fans at the time as they continue to rally against owners BlueCo, who run the multi-club group including Chelsea.

Emegha was not only the Strasbourg top scorer last term with 14 goals in 27 appearances – he managed eight from 28 the year before – but is also the skipper.



That did not help ease worries from fans, who saw their main man posing in a Chelsea kit at the Cobham training ground whilst still contracted to Strasbourg.

Emegha has struggled for form and fitness this season, only playing 10 Ligue 1 games.

He helped lead the team into Europe but barely contributed to their progress once there.

Manager O’Neil, who replaced Liam Rosenior in charge in January after he was poached by Chelsea, has seen the season go from promising history to on the verge of collapse.

Six defeats in the last eight games in all competitions have plunged Strasbourg into mid-table, now unlikely to make even the Conference League next season.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Last month some Strasbourg ultras joined Chelsea fans in their protest against the Clearlake Capital-Todd Boehly consortium.

They have been voicing their anger at the American-based owners ever since the takeover in 2023.

Sports.title: Chelsea legend Eden Hazard reveals bizarre new career path with major investment in the ‘Facebook of sport’
Sports.content:
EDEN HAZARD has swapped technique for tech bros – with the Chelsea icon investing in a startup dubbed the Facebook of sport.

The Belgium midfielder showed his sublime skills during seven years at Stamford Bridge, winning both the Premier League and Europa League twice.





Hazard scored 110 goals in 352 games, and also lifted the FA Cup and League Cup before leaving for Real Madrid in 2019.

He retired in 2023 after an injury-plagued spell at the Bernabeu, and has since kept a low profile.

But the 35-year-old has now become an investor and ambassador for Belgian online platform Opportunity Players.

The site offers athletes in all sports the chance to link up with clubs, and is also open to managers, coaches, physios and nutritionists.



Hazard’s former Belgium teammate Laurent Ciman, 40, manages the service from his base in north America.

Fellow Red Devil, Girona defender Axel Witsel, 37 has also invested in the business.

And ex-Tottenham and West Brom winger Nacer Chadli, 36, is listed on Opportunity Players’ website among its supporters.

Hazard hailed the service, insisting: “It is unique. Nothing like this existed before, and we have created it.”



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

Chief executive Christel Cherain added: “Opportunity Players is a community that makes respect, safety and the common good its top priorities.

“We offer space to everyone who wants to pursue their dreams.”

The site already has 40,000 users, and aims for a MILLION by next year after expanding into China, South America and north Africa.



Belgian media have already acclaimed it as sport’s answer to LinkedIn or Facebook.

In addition to that, the former Chelsea star also owns a wine business, as well as taking part in various charity matches and mega bike rides since retirement.

Sports.title: Crystal Palace make audacious bid to appoint Frank Lampard, 47, with London rivals also interested in Coventry boss
Sports.content:
CRYSTAL PALACE have made an audacious move to make Frank Lampard their new manager.

SunSport understands the Conference League finalists sounded out the Coventry boss about replacing Oliver Glasner at Selhurst Park.





Prem rivals Fulham have also shown interest in Lampard if current chief Marco Silva leaves when his contract expires this summer.

But Palace, who are on their way to Leipzig for their first Euro final against Rayo Vallecano on May 27, have made their first move for Lampard.

The in-demand 47-year-old masterminded Coventry’s promotion to the Prem after a 25-year wait.

Palace were alerted as ex-Chelsea, Everton and Derby manager Lampard is weighing up his options after winning the Championship title.



The former England midfield star is aware that Sky Blues owner Doug King is unlikely to have the resources to help safeguard the club’s newly gained top-flight status.

King himself has openly admitted that he may struggle to hang onto his prized managerial asset this summer.

Although Lampard still has 12 months of his current contract to run and will be offered an improved one it’s unlikely that a realistic King will stand in his way if he is tempted elsewhere.

Palace believe that under Lampard they can continue the success Glasner has brought to Selhurst Park by winning last year’s FA Cup – which secured European football – and the Community Shield.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Lampard also knows that the Eagles, who have already been turned down by departing Bournemouth boss Andoni Iraola, represent a good opportunity for him to make an impact back in the Prem.

Glasner’s Palace reached the Conference final on Thursday night after beating Ukrainian side Shakhtar Donetsk 2-1 to seal a 5-2 aggregate triumph

Sports.title: Euro giants’ fans banned from ever attending stadium again with much-loved 16,003-seater arena to be demolished
Sports.content:
FORMER European Cup finalists Panathinaikos will play their last ever home match in their historic ground behind closed doors.

PAO competed in the 1971 final of Uefa’s premiere competition against Ajax at Wembley where they lost 2-0.





The Greek giants achieved that historic feat by winning some big matches in their iconic stadium of Apostolos Nikolaidis, also known as Leoforos, heading to the big game in London against Johan Cruyff and co.

However, the Athenian outfit will leave their 16,003-capacity stadium at the end of the season.

And Panathinaikos fans won’t be able to bid their beloved stadium a proper farewell in the team’s final home match.

Rafa Benitez‘s side was slapped with a one-game fan ban following troubles during Sunday’s derby against rivals AEK Athens.



The sanction was handed out after home supporters launched firecrackers and flares onto the pitch.

Thus, Panathinaikos’ next and final home game on May 17 against PAOK will take place in an empty Leoforos.

The former Champions League club will play all of their domestic matches in Athens’ Olympic Stadium, also known as OAKA, next season.

Panathinaikos have spent the last couple of decades alternating between Leoforos and the Olympic venue, which is the largest stadium in Greece with a total capacity of 75,000.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

In fact, Benitez’s men spent this season playing all of their domestic home matches at Leoforos and their European fixtures at OAKA.

Panathinaikos are expected to move to their new state-of-the-art stadium at Votanikos, which will hold 39,074, in May 2027.

And Leoforos is expected to be demolished once the transition is finalised, but there is currently no definite timeline as the move has already been postponed a couple of times.

Panathinaikos will look to relive their glorious history which has seen them winning 20 league titles and 20 Greek Cup trophies since their creation in 1908.

PAO also enjoyed tremendous success in Europe as they made it to the Champions League semi-finals in 1985 and 1996 as well as the quarter-finals in 1992 and 2002.



In addition, Panathinaikos made the Europa League quarter-finals in 1988 and 2003.

Sports.title: England’s most isolated club asks to be relegated after travelling over 7000 miles for matches
Sports.content:
ENGLAND’s most isolated club has requested to be relegated after travelling thousands of miles for matches.

Mousehole AFC is hoping to play in the South West Peninsula League for the 2026/27 season.





The division is one below the Southern League Division One South during the recent season.

Mousehole is based less than ten miles from Land’s End in Cornwall and is the most westerly football club in the English National League system

Their isolated location leaves them with mega journeys for the majority of their away fixtures.

Throughout the 2025-26 season, Mousehole racked up 7,000miles from their travels.



As a result, the toll the travel takes on the club’s resources has left them requesting to be relegated.

The club confirmed the request for voluntary relegation had been made in a statement.

An extract read: “Following careful consideration, Mousehole AFC can confirm that the club is proposing a strategic reset by applying for voluntary relegation from the Southern League Division One South and seeking entry into the South West Peninsula League for the 2026/27 season.

“After reviewing all options, the board believes that taking a step back now provides the best platform to rebuild on stronger and more sustainable foundations for the future.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“Over the past decade, Mousehole AFC has been on one of the most remarkable journeys in Cornish football.

“Together, players, staff, volunteers, supporters and sponsors have helped take a small village club in West Cornwall to a level many thought impossible.

“Along the way, we have celebrated league titles, unforgettable occasions, national recognition, and created a football club that has become one of the most recognised and respected in Cornwall.

“The club would like to place on record its heartfelt thanks to everyone who has contributed to that journey.



“From volunteers and supporters to players, coaches, sponsors and local businesses, this rise simply would not have been possible without the dedication, belief and commitment of so many people across our community.”

Mousehole gained attention after being visited by Prince Williams in November 2025.

The royal has helped build a road to help improve access to the club.

Club chairman Deryk Heywood has insisted the request is the correct decision.

He believes that it will help protect the long-term interests of the Penzance-based club.



He said: “Mousehole AFC has always tried to do the right thing, not simply the easy thing.

South West Peninsula League statement HERE is the statement released by the SWP League in response to Mousehole's request for relegation... “The Board of the South West Peninsula League note the application to join the league from Mousehole AFC and, as always, are supportive of clubs in our unique geographical location and well aware of the issues they face. “We of course await the FA allocations which will confirm the make-up of both our divisions and these are expected around the middle of the month. “The league however wishes to clarify its position in regard to the sustainability of clubs within the National League System. “The recent application from Helston Athletic, the issues surrounding St Austell and now this application clearly show that a “one size fits all” pyramid structure is unsustainable in isolated rural areas. “We stand ready to assist individual clubs experiencing issues AND to be part of a longer-term solution to keeping non-league football sustainable in our region and to this end are in constant dialogue with The FA & its leagues committee.”

“This decision reflects our commitment to protecting the long-term future of the football club and building something sustainable for our players, supporters and wider community.

“We are incredibly proud of what has been achieved over the last few years.

“The journey this club has been on has been extraordinary.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“But now is the time to regroup, reconnect with our community roots, and make sure that whatever comes next is built to last.

“This is not the end of ambition at Mousehole AFC. It is the beginning of a new chapter.”

Sports.title: Pregnant widow of former Man Utd starlet ‘so proud’ as she leads emotional charity walk one year after his tragic death
Sports.content:
ONE year after Joe Thompson’s death, his pregnant widow organised a charity walk in his memory, carrying the son he dreamt of.

SunSport joined 250 people – including travellers from all over the world – on an inspiring 15-mile trek from Rochdale FC to Old Trafford in honour of Joe.





Joe died of Hodgkin’s lymphoma at the age of 36 in April last year after his third cancer diagnosis in a decade, having twice recovered during a playing career that started at Manchester United’s academy.

Months before his death, he led hundreds on a 21-mile walk from Gary Neville’s Hotel Football to Dale’s Crown Oil Arena ground to raise awareness of cancer treatments.

This year’s route was symbolically set at 15 miles to honour Joe’s Rochdale jersey—a number the club officially retired after the midfielder’s passing.

On Saturday his wife Chantelle and daughter Lula, 13, led a march with friends and family to raise funds for the Joe Thompson Foundation.



Chantelle is currently 29 weeks pregnant with Joe’s baby, conceived on her first IVF attempt using a frozen embryo since his passing.

The pregnancy follows a devastating fertility journey that saw the full-term loss of their son, Dre, in 2020, before the “miracle” natural conception of their daughter, Athena, in 2024.

Chantelle said: “He would have been so proud of this. I can just see his face now, smiling from ear to ear. The baby just means absolutely everything.

“I know it’s never going to replace Joe obviously. Joe is Joe. But to be able to bring his baby into the world again is beautiful.”



Her husband even gave Chantelle the name for the baby boy he predicted, but she is keeping it private.

She added: “He actually had a vision of us sitting outside with a baby boy. This was maybe six months before he passed, and he assumed that it was all of us.

“And then maybe two weeks before he passed, we were just sitting in the garden and he just had a realisation and was like, ‘I think I was watching you with the baby and the girls in the garden, not me physically here with you.



“It’s crazy because if Athena was not conceived naturally, I probably wouldn’t have had the embryo now.”

Joe trained at United’s academy from the age of nine and played professionally for Tranmere Rovers, Rochdale, Carlisle, Southport and Bury.

At the age of 23, he was diagnosed with blood cancer and returned to playing following six months of treatment.

The cancer returned three years later and in March 2024 he was diagnosed for the third time, with the disease spreading to his lungs.

Joe’s close friend Aaron Burns played a key role in organising the walk, with his phone number on the maps handed out in case anybody got lost.



Burns, who is the lead trustee for United’s former player union (AFMUP) said: “Football introduced us, but friendship kept us together.

“We met at Carrington, I was 11, he was 10. And he was just a young boy that loved football, but radiated energy.

“United is more than a football club. It’s a community, it’s a feeling, it’s a spirit and the spirit of Man United is here today. We stayed close until the end.”



Burns and I caught up with former United player Fraizer Campbell on the first leg between Rochdale and Bury.

Ever the team player, Campbell handed out sweets “for energy” just after rescuing a group of walkers who were about to take a wrong turn.

Walking past the newsagent’s Joe grew up next to, Campbell said: “It’s incredible to carry on his legacy, to see people who never met him during his life be here today is out of this world.

“I also met him at Carrington and our families remained close. We all miss him so much.”

United released Joe in 2005 when he was 16, before he made his senior debut with Rochdale at 17.



Aarons joined Cardiff later, and Campbell went on to make four first-team appearances before a successful career across the Premier League and EFL.

Joe, who was born in Bath, moved to Rochdale as a boy to live with his aunt and shone in sports at St Vincent’s primary school, before catching the eye of United.

Yet his impact on Greater Manchester went far beyond football—Joe dedicated himself to uplifting the community and improving the lives of those around him.

Former Love Island star and friend Scott Thomas joined the walk for a second successive year.



Thomas, who first met Joe on the Manchester party scene, said: “He had a massive impact on my life.

“He always pushed me out of my comfort zone. I wanted to be here today to make sure I’m keeping his energy alive because he was such a huge inspiration.

“No matter how ill he was, he devoted so much energy into helping people. He is someone I could never forget.”

Joe also predicted a major life event for Thomas – meeting his girlfriend Lauren.

Thomas explained: “He pushed me to go on Dr Jodie Spencer’s retreat in Nashville and said ‘you’ll meet your future wifey there’.



“And it’s crazy because I’m actually here today with my new girlfriend who I met from going to that retreat!”

Joe also checked in with Thomas before and after his second stint on Love Island in January 2025 to make sure “he was doing it for the right reasons”.

Among his career highlights, Joe’s dramatic winner saved Rochdale from relegation from League Two against Charlton Athletic on 5 May 2018, a year after his second cancer diagnosis.

His sport psychologist Robert Martin-Hall met Joe before his first cancer diagnosis at age 23 in November 2013, when he was at Tranmere.



Martin-Hall said: “When I first met Joe I asked him about his career goals, and he said his wanted to score a ‘goal of significance’.

“A goal that would be shown on TV and be remembered for years to come.

“When he scored that goal for Rochdale, after all of the recovery, he text me saying: ‘Eight years’

“It gave him heroes status. It had been eight years since he set that goal and it was being shown on Sky Sports News and the BBC that evening.”

Joe hung up his boots in 2019 and transitioned into a career in media as a pundit, motivational speaker, and mental health advocate.



Chantelle picked up Joe’s honorary doctorate in football psychology on his behalf at the Emirates Stadium last year.

Meanwhile, United player Ella Toone met walkers inside Hotel Football opposite Old Trafford after returning from a four-month injury to play in the women’s 1-1 draw against Brighton.

Toone’s partner Joe Bunney, who played with and against Joe in his career, was a vocal and leading presence on the walk.

He told SunSport: “When I came to Rochdale he was picking me up from the train station every day because I didn’t drive for like five years.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“But that Rochdale goal actually relegated me because I had moved to Northampton! So I used to remind him of that.”



In fact, an Instagram post by Toone promoting the walk reached United fan Caroline living in Malta, who flew over 1,200 miles to join in.

Sports.title: Former world champions’ clash abandoned after one minute as fans invade pitch and burn their own stadium
Sports.content:
A FOOTBALL game involving former world champions Flamengo was abandoned after just one minute following a protest by rival fans against their club’s owners.

Brazilian giants Flamengo were paying a visit to Colombian rivals Independiente Medellin in the fourth game in the group stage of the Copa Libertadores – South America’s Champions League.





However, the clash had to be abandoned just after kick-off as home fans at the Gigante de la Montaña stadium launched an incredible protest.

Fans were seen throwing objects and lighting flares in their seats while others stormed the field of play.

It even caused a fire in the centre of one of the stands, while a banner harshly criticising the players and football governing bodies Dimayor (Colombia), Conmebol and Fifa was also revealed.

ESPN Brazil also reported one of their reporter’s backpacks had caught fire after missiles had been thrown by fans, while the cameraman’s equipment and trousers were also set alight.

Supporter anger had come following the club’s elimination from the Liga Dimayor Apertura Tournament playoffs following a 2-1 home loss to Águilas Doradas.

Owner Raúl Giraldo had also been seen making obscene gestures that only made matters worse, before announcing his resignation from his legal representation, with fans demanding the removal of the entire management team.

Security officials had requested the club play behind closed doors due to the rising discontent in the fanbase, but that request was denied by club chiefs.

Police were present to prevent a full-scale pitch invasion behind one of the goals.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Venezuelan referee Jesús Valenzuela had stopped the game with one minute 50 on the clock, with teams returning to their locker rooms after five minutes.

The stadium announcer then told fans to leave the ground after 10 minutes.



Conmebol are now set to launch an investigation which could determine the outcome of the match and potentially award a 3-0 win to Flamengo.

They beat Liverpool in the 1981 Intercontinental Cup final 3-0 off the back of a stunning performance by iconic midfielder Zico.

Sports.content:
Arsenal handed new Premier League title advantage as Man City dealt double fixture blow

Arsenal are favourites for the Premier League title and their chances of triumphing may have increased with Manchester City dealt a nightmare fixture scenario

View 2 Images Arsenal have been handed three Premier League title boosts at Manchester City's expense (Image: (Photo by Catherine Ivill - AMA/Getty Images))

Arsenal appear to have received three distinct Premier League title advantages over Manchester City. Last weekend, the Gunners seized control of the title battle by defeating Fulham while City drew at Everton, and now Thursday evening's European results have handed the leaders a clear edge.

‌



Firstly, with Aston Villa reaching the Europa League final against Freiburg, sixth position in the Premier League can now guarantee Champions League football. To offer the likes of Brentford, Brighton, Bournemouth and Chelsea that chance, Villa must prevail in Istanbul and finish fifth.

‌



Two of Man City's remaining four opponents are Brentford and Bournemouth, and they face them both before Villa's European final, which provides them with extra motivation to attempt to claim points off Guardiola's side.

With fixtures on either side of that midweek encounter, squad rotation is a possibility, though it will almost certainly be more significant against Arsenal, given that Palace have a Conference League final against Rayo Vallecano just days afterwards.

Sports.content:
Jadon Sancho snaps back at Man Utd fans after Aston Villa reach Europa League final

Jadon Sancho made a cameo appearance during Aston Villa's 4-1 win against Nottingham Forest on Thursday which sent Unai Emery's side through to the Europa League final

View 3 Images Jadon Sancho didn't hold back (Image: Jean Catuffe/Getty Images)

Jadon Sancho has fired back at Manchester United fans who mocked his contribution to Aston Villa's run to the Europa League final. Sancho, 26, took to social media while celebrating Villa's 4-1 victory over Nottingham Forest, as they made home advantage count in their semi-final second leg on Thursday.

‌



The winger has now reached a European final in each of the last three seasons, all during loan spells away from United. Sancho played in the Champions League final with Borussia Dortmund in 2024 before helping Chelsea win the Conference League final last year.

‌



After the feat was posted on social media platform X, however, a United fan took a swipe. "Let's have a quick look at @Sanchooo10's input in getting to those finals," they posted.

‌



Sancho - who's featured in 12 of Villa's 14 Europa League games, scoring one goal - replied at 11.09pm: "Yeah, make sure you have a good look!"

Another user defended Sancho by claiming that his performance against Paris Saint-Germain left-back Nuno Mendes in the 2024 Champions League semi-finals had been forgotten. The United loanee replied to with a shrugging emoji.

‌



One United supporter took umbrage with his contribution this season, saying: "Made a European final playing absolutely no part (he come on for 4 minutes tonight) and he's suddenly acting as if he's (Kylian) Mbappe. Shows his weak & poor mentality, m***."

Sports.title: 5,000-1: The Leicester City Fairytale – New documentary on Premier League's greatest shock
Sports.content:
With the 10th anniversary of Leicester City's Premier League title triumph coinciding with their descent to a new low, one question has been asked repeatedly over recent days and weeks. Would their supporters, if posed the question back in 2015, have accepted claiming their first top-flight championship in exchange for hitting rock bottom a decade on?

The knee-jerk response is yes, without a doubt. The more considered response is that it's a pointless question. There was no Faustian pact. Success and failure don't necessarily arrive as a pair.

This isn't simply a case of football's natural ebb and flow, where lean spells are bound to follow golden eras. Leicester made a string of costly errors to squander the strong position they had built.

Nobody anticipated a title defence, yet there was every opportunity for the club to cement itself as a consistent contender for European football. They've thrown it away spectacularly. Their 10-year plunge from top-flight champions to the third tier is the second fastest in English football history, behind only Derby's nine-year collapse.

‌



Nevertheless, there's little value in dwelling on that squandered opportunity. Nothing will change the fact that Leicester will be lining up in League One next season.

The real question that needs addressing is: what does being the 2016 Premier League champions actually mean for Leicester City now they find themselves in League One? Viewed through a pessimistic prism, it could become a millstone. It's the ultimate peak, never to be surpassed by City or any other club. No bookmaker will ever again offer odds of 5,000-1 on a Premier League side to claim the title.

Regarded as this insurmountable moment, it could become a burden that weighs the club down. The summit has been reached. What's the point in pushing for more?

However, look at it differently and couldn't it serve as a wellspring of motivation? This is arguably the greatest feat in English football. Why not harness that?

‌



As you can witness in our new documentary, 5,000-1: The Leicester City Fairytale, that season was enchanting. Whenever the tale is revisited, the feelings come rushing back. Watching the strikes, hearing Claudio Ranieri's press conference quotes, imagining the atmosphere inside the King Power Stadium and across the city during those nine months, they send waves of euphoria through your system.

Looking back on episodes from the campaign, whether crucial to the championship triumph or intimate and individual, can help supporters break free from the despair and negativity.

Yet they don't want their happiness to purely be about looking backwards. They want to live through positive times alongside those recollections. But perhaps the narrative of the title victory can galvanise future generations of Leicester squads.

‌



This is the club and the city where the unattainable was attained. This is the venue where the impossible transformed into reality. Why not have faith in the optimal result when there's evidence they can deliver it. For next season, they're back to where the title-winning journey began.

There's a case to be made the road to glory started when Ranieri took charge. Maybe it was Andy King's late winner against West Ham in the opening match of the great escape. Some might argue it was Robert Huth's loan arrival from Stoke in January 2015.

King Power's takeover could be the true beginning. But trace it right back and the real starting point was the club dropping into League One for the first time in their history.

View 2 Images Leicester City's Premier League title win was the upset that no-one expected

‌



Following a string of lower-half Championship finishes, relegation offered the opportunity to tear everything up and begin afresh. They'd been treading water. It was time to reshape, reorganise, reconfigure. And that's exactly what they did.

So eight years after a goalless draw at Stoke sent them down to the third tier, Andrea Bocelli walked onto the King Power Stadium pitch to perform Nessun Dorma and Wes Morgan lifted the Premier League trophy aloft.

It's a tale to be immensely proud of and it's a tale that can keep the fire burning. It's a tale that can inspire, that can ignite belief, that can help defy the odds. Because this is where it all unfolded.

As Leicester prepare for life in League One and a sense of despair looms over the club, it's worth taking stock of that Premier League title triumph. Not in terms of what followed and the missed opportunities but in terms of what can be achieved from such an improbable position.

‌



They find themselves back where it all started. The greatest heights can still be scaled from here. There's living proof of that in Leicester, after all.

Sports.title: Ruben Amorim's transfer rule that Man Utd must keep with new manager
Sports.content:
Ruben Amorim's transfer rule that Man Utd must keep with new manager

Former Manchester United manager Ruben Amorim outlined a crucial part of the club's recruitment plans last year

View 2 Images Ruben Amorim spoke about a key aspect of transfers during his time at Manchester United (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Manchester United may have thrived since Ruben Amorim left the club but the former boss did address a key part of the club’s recruitment strategy. The Portuguese coach focused on identifying the right personalities in the transfer window, providing a blueprint for his permanent successor to follow.

‌



Michael Carrick has taken the reins at Old Trafford since Amorim’s departure in January. The interim boss has won 10 of his 14 matches in charge, leading to clamour for him to be given the role permanently.

‌



The manager’s job is just one of several key decisions that the club must make this summer. United have secured their place in next season’s Champions League and will need to sign several players who can help the team compete on multiple fronts.

‌



Last summer, United focused on improving their attacking options, bringing in the trio of Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Benjamin Sesko, as well as new goalkeeper Senne Lammens. However, former United boss Amorim admitted at the time that the club were not solely looking at what their transfer targets could add to the team on the pitch.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

“‘It’s a key point in our way of doing things now. It’s not just how they play,” Amorim said in August 2025.

‌



OPINION Abbie Meehan Man United's dream XI next season as Real Madrid star and £100million midfielder both join

“It’s really important how they play, of course, because that is the job, but the character is really important and we took a lot of time to know the players, to talk with everybody before we bring some players to our group.

“That is going to be like a rule and it’s going to be massive in our decision when we bring the player.”

‌



Although Amorim was unable to get the best out of his United squad, their resurgence under Carrick has shown the group’s togetherness. The 44-year-old began his tenure with statement wins over Manchester City and Arsenal, while their recent victory over Liverpool secured Champions League football.

Despite not yet deciding on a permanent manager, United have already begun planning for the future by giving new contracts to Harry Maguire and Kobbie Mainoo. Interim boss Carrick will know what the duo bring to the squad away from the pitch and has already stated that he has been involved in discussions about United’s next steps.

View 2 Images Manchester United manager Michael Carrick has been a success this season (Image: Shaun Brooks - CameraSport via Getty Images)

‌



Speaking last month, Carrick explained: “Certainly, in the role I’m in, there’s decisions that need taking care of. I said it as soon as I came here - I’m part of that and whatever that looks like moving forward, I’m part of that.

“I’m trying to improve things and make things better all the time. Certainly there’s conversations in different directions and different things that I’m definitely part of. And I think it should be that way anyway, because things need done. So I’m here to take care of that.”

United must retain the same team spirit if they are to continue progressing and challenge for major honours. Whether he remains United boss or not, Carrick is perfectly placed to spot those character traits in the transfer market and follow the rule that Amorim outlined last year.

Sports.content:
Virgil van Dijk to receive imminent offer with Liverpool star 'ready to leave'

Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk has been linked with a surprise move away from Anfield this summer, despite his contract still having one year left to run

View 2 Images Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk is reportedly a transfer target for Galatasaray this summer. (Image: 2026 James Gill - Danehouse)

Liverpool captain Virgil van Dijk could be set for an imminent offer from Turkish side Galatasaray in the summer transfer window. Turkish outlet FotoMac claim the Dutch international is 'ready to leave' Anfield and he could yet join Mohamed Salah in leaving the club on a free transfer once the season ends.

‌



The report claims Van Dijk is assessing his Liverpool future, following the club's disappointing campaign. The 34-year-old has one year left on his current Reds' contract, having agreed an extension last season, but is aware of the club's plans to sign younger players.

‌



The Reds signed Giovanni Leoni last summer and have agreed a deal with Rennes to sign youngster Jeremy Jacquet, while they're also in talks to extend Ibrahima Konate's deal, which expires this summer.

‌



FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

The report adds Van Dijk has been impressed by Galatasaray on the two occasions he's visited the Turkish outfit in the Champions League this season, with boss Okan Buruk keen on bolstering his options in the heart of defence.

Andy Robertson and Salah are two of the senior stars set to leave Anfield on free transfers this summer, and the report claims Van Dijk could follow suit.

‌



They suggest Van Dijk could even terminate his contract in order to join the Turkish Super Lig club, just as Salah is doing in order to pursue other options.

View 2 Images Virgil van Dijk. (Image: Getty Images)

However, Van Dijk's recent comments about Liverpool's rebuild suggest he's committed to the club until the end of his contract, admitting the Reds needed to put in a lot of work over the summer.

‌



"It has been ups and downs," Van Dijk said reflecting on this season. "Some wins have felt good. Winning feels good. But we can’t build on that and it has been the story of our season. That is what is difficult.

"Just to go up and down in your emotions is never a good thing. When you win, it’s happy days. When you lose, it is bad and you are held accountable. You have to take responsibility. It’s just life.

"I think it’s unacceptable that we have lost too many times as defending champions of the Premier League and we shouldn’t accept it whatsoever. There will be a lot of work that has to be done going into next season.

Article continues below

"When I am back from the World Cup, I will go into it. But there is a lot of work to do be done behind the scenes."
